title: Anointing of the sick
hook: not only for the dying; oil for anyone seriously ill or old (CCC 1514)

segments.voice: Yesterday, reconciliation, the sacrament of return. Your line was there's always a way back. Did you take one small step toward someone? Day one hundred thirty.

A hospital room, late afternoon. A woman in her seventies is going in for heart surgery tomorrow. Her daughter has called the parish, and a priest comes in with a small oil stock in his pocket, the size of a lipstick. The daughter looks nervous. Isn't this, she whispers, what they do when someone's dying? The priest smiles. It's a common mix-up. Her mother isn't dying. She's sick, and scared, and that's exactly who this is for. Today, the anointing of the sick.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM, THE DAY BEFORE.` → `ISN'T THIS FOR THE DYING?` → `IT'S FOR THE SICK.`

segments.voice: For a long time this sacrament was called extreme unction, the last anointing, and in practice it was often saved for the very end. So some people still think of it that way: the priest arrives, and it's time to say goodbye. After the Second Vatican Council, the Church changed the name and the emphasis. It's the anointing of the sick, and the Catechism says it's for anyone who begins to be in danger of death from sickness or old age. Not dying: beginning to be in danger. Before major surgery. When a chronic illness gets worse. When age makes a person frail. And it can be received again, if the illness returns or worsens. The roots are in the letter of James. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." James goes on to say the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. The priest lays his hands on the person's head in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands with the oil of the sick, blessed by the bishop. Only a priest can give it. What do Catholics believe it does? Strength, peace and courage to face the illness, union with Christ's own suffering, forgiveness, and sometimes, if God wills, bodily healing. It doesn't replace doctors. Catholics go to both. When someone is truly near death, the priest may also hear their confession and give Communion, called viaticum, food for the journey. Those together are what people mean by last rites.
screen: `NOT ONLY THE LAST ANOINTING.` · `IS ANY MAN SICK AMONG YOU?` · `HANDS, OIL, FOREHEAD AND PALMS.` · `STRENGTH, PEACE, AND SOMETIMES HEALING.` · then, large: `THE SICK ARE NOT FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who is ill. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is sick or in the hospital, or very old and frail. See their face. Picture the room they're in. If you know what they're afraid of, hold that too. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't pray, simply keep them company in your mind for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Extreme unction. The old name for anointing of the sick, oil on the forehead and hands, for anyone seriously ill or old, not only the dying. Today's word.
Your line: the sick are not forgotten. Today, send one message, or make one call, to someone who is ill. Ask how they are, and then listen. Day one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: A Catholic who is seriously ill, frail with age or facing major surgery can ask a priest for the anointing, at home, in hospital, or at a parish Mass for the sick; it can be received more than once.

original.note: Greek: olive oil, the word in James 5:14 for the oil used to anoint the sick.

trapdoor: what you thought: the last rites, when it's time to say goodbye.
what it means: a sacrament for the seriously ill or old, for strength, peace, forgiveness and sometimes healing.
what a scholar hears: once called extreme unction; after Vatican II renamed and reopened to the seriously ill, rooted in James 5:14–15.

sources.quoted: Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.

notes: CCC 1514 paraphrased ('begins to be in danger of death from sickness or old age'). Confirm the wording 'begins to be in danger because of serious illness or old age'.
Rite: silent laying on of hands, anointing forehead and hands (Paul VI, Sacram unctionem infirmorum, 1972). Confirm.
Oil of the sick blessed at the Chrism Mass; a priest may bless oil in necessity. Simplified. Confirm.
Last rites as confession, anointing and viaticum: common usage. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the Catechism paraphrase had dropped 'of death' from CCC 1514; restored, with a line that keeps the day's point (beginning to be in danger, not dying). Cut 'for centuries', 'once a year', 'many people still think', and the odd suggestion to say 'is any man sick among you' as a prayer. This day keeps the remember-someone-ill practice; days 116 and 121 were changed so it no longer repeats them.
